title: How to Make Ghevar at Home: The Rajasthani Sweet Perfect for Raksha Bandhan
excerpt: With Raksha Bandhan a day away, here is a step-by-step guide to making this honeycomb-textured Rajasthani festive dessert in your own kitchen.
body:
• Ghevar is a traditional Rajasthani dessert with a distinctive honeycomb texture, closely associated with the festivals of Teej and Raksha Bandhan during the monsoon season.
  • The sweet traces its roots to the royal kitchens of Jaipur and is traditionally gifted to newly married daughters by their parents on the day before Teej.
  • Making ghevar at home requires a cold, thin batter poured from a height into hot ghee — the temperature contrast creates its signature porous, lattice-like structure.
  • Variations include malai ghevar topped with rabri, mawa ghevar, and modern twists, though the classic sugar-syrup-soaked version remains the most popular.

With Raksha Bandhan falling on August 28 this year, sweet shops across Rajasthan and North India are stacked with golden discs of ghevar — the honeycomb-textured dessert that has been a fixture of monsoon celebrations for centuries. For NRIs marking the festival far from family, making ghevar at home can turn a kitchen into a small piece of Rajasthan.

The dessert looks deceptively complex with its porous, lace-like structure, but requires just a handful of ingredients and one crucial technique: pouring cold batter from a height into hot ghee. Master that, and the rest follows.

A Sweet With Royal Roots

Ghevar's origins trace back to the royal kitchens of Jaipur, Bikaner, and Udaipur, where court chefs crafted the dessert for Rajasthan's maharajas, according to food historians. The word itself comes from the Sanskrit "ghritapura" — "ghrita" meaning ghee and "pura" meaning cake — a fitting name for a sweet built entirely from clarified butter.

The dessert is traditionally associated with the Hindu month of Shraavana and the festivals of Teej and Raksha Bandhan. In Rajasthani households, it is the first gift a daughter receives from her parental home after marriage, sent as part of a Sindhara hamper on the day before Gangaur and Teej. The 16th-century poet saint Mira Bai referenced offering ghevar to Lord Krishna in her poems, and the sweet remains one of the 56 dishes in the Chhapan Bhog served to the deity.

Ghevar even reached international audiences when Depinder Chhibber served it during her audition for MasterChef Australia Season 13, introducing the dessert to viewers unfamiliar with Indian monsoon sweets.

What You Will Need

"The word itself comes from the Sanskrit "ghritapura" — "ghrita" meaning ghee and "pura" meaning cake — a fitting name for a sweet built entirely from clarified butter."

This recipe, shared by chef Bharti Sanghi of Life Artisanal Food with Hindustan Times, uses curd for a lighter batter.

For the batter: 1 cup all-purpose flour (maida), 1 tablespoon gram flour (besan), half a cup of curd, half a cup plus half a litre of ice-cold water, 6 ice cubes, and ghee plus oil for deep frying.

For the sugar syrup: One-and-a-half cups sugar, three-quarters cup water, 3 cardamom pods, and 1 teaspoon lemon juice.

For garnishing: Chopped almonds, pistachios, edible silver leaf (varak), and rabri (optional).

Preparing the Batter

The batter is the foundation. Blend the curd, ghee, half a cup of water, and ice cubes until creamy. Add the flour and half the remaining water, blend again, then add the gram flour and the rest of the water. The final consistency should be very thin and pourable — thinner than pancake batter. Refrigerate until needed.

Keeping the batter cold is essential. The temperature contrast between the chilled batter and the hot oil is what creates ghevar's signature honeycomb structure. The colder the batter, the more dramatic the splattering effect that forms those intricate air pockets.

The Frying Technique

This is where patience pays off. Use a small, deep saucepan — the size of the pan determines the size of your ghevar. Fill it less than halfway with a mix of ghee and oil, and heat until very hot.

Take a small ladleful of batter and pour it from a height of about six inches, directly into the center of the pan. The ghee will foam up and the batter will spread to the sides, forming a lacy web. Let each layer cook before adding the next ladleful. Continue building layers until the ghevar reaches your desired height and the edges turn golden. Reduce the flame toward the end and cook until crisp throughout.

A word of caution: the hot ghee splatters. Wearing gloves and using a pointed pouring utensil like a milk pitcher, rather than an open ladle, helps keep hands safe.

Sugar Syrup and Finishing

While the ghevar fries, prepare the sugar syrup by combining sugar, water, cardamom pods, and lemon juice in a saucepan. Bring to a boil, then simmer. The syrup should reach a one-string consistency — when pressed between thumb and forefinger and pulled apart, a single thread forms.

Drain the fried ghevar carefully and soak it in the warm sugar syrup for about one minute on each side. Handle gently — the cooked disc is fragile and can crumble easily. Remove to a plate and garnish with chopped nuts and edible silver paper. For malai ghevar, add a generous layer of chilled rabri on top.

Variations and Serving Tips

The classic plain ghevar soaked in sugar syrup is the purest version. Malai ghevar, topped with rabri and saffron-infused cream, is the richer cousin popular at celebrations. Mawa ghevar incorporates reduced milk solids for a denser texture. Modern sweet shops have added chocolate and other toppings, though purists maintain the dessert's beauty lies in its simplicity.

Ghevar is best eaten fresh, within a few hours of frying. If making ahead, store the unsyruped discs in an airtight container and soak them in warm syrup just before serving. For NRIs attempting this for the first time, the key is to not rush the layering process — each ladleful of batter needs time to set before the next pour.
image_caption: A ghevar topped with malai and garnished with nuts, a traditional Rajasthani sweet. The honeycomb-textured dessert is a staple of Teej and Raksha Bandhan celebrations across North India.
nri_angle: Making traditional Indian sweets at home connects NRIs to their heritage during festive occasions like Raksha Bandhan, when distance from family is felt most acutely.
